transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I guess I’m here because this elevator thing has started taking over more of my day than I want to admit. I mean, I’ve been planning around not using them, like at home I’ll take five flights of stairs instead, every time, even if I’m tired or carrying stuff.

And it’s not just that—I turned down a workshop recently because it was in a high-rise, and I just kept thinking about the elevator situation instead of the workshop itself. I also stopped visiting one of my older computer students, which I feel bad about, because his building doesn’t really have another option besides the elevator. So… yeah, it’s starting to interfere with normal things, and I figured I should probably talk to someone about it.
Do you feel anxious when you think about using an elevator?

Yeah, I do. Even just thinking about using one can set me off a bit. It’s strange because logically I know, like, an elevator in an office building is probably safe. I’m not walking around thinking every modern elevator is actually dangerous or anything.

But when I’m standing in front of those older elevator doors—like the ones in my apartment building, or sometimes at work—it’s like my brain doesn’t care what I know. It immediately jumps to, “What if I get trapped in there?” or “What if it drops?” And I know that sounds dramatic when I say it out loud, like obviously people use them all day and nothing happens, but in the moment it feels very real. Part of me is aware I’m probably overreacting, but another part of me is already treating it like I’m about to step into something unsafe.
Do you experience similar anxiety or fear in situations other than using elevators?

Not really, no. I mean, I can get nervous about normal stuff like anyone—work things, maybe meeting new people, that kind of thing—but it doesn’t feel like this. The elevator thing is very specific. It’s really the idea of being inside one, especially if it’s older or feels enclosed, and not being able to just get out.

I’ve tried to think if there’s some bigger pattern, like small spaces in general or heights or crowds or something, but I don’t think so. I don’t walk around feeling scared of everything. It’s mainly elevators that seem to flip that switch for me.
Do you feel anxious or uncomfortable in other small or enclosed spaces, like cars or tunnels?

I don’t think so, at least not in the same way. Like, I drive and ride in cars without really thinking about it. I mean, if traffic is bad or someone’s driving aggressively, I might be annoyed or tense, but it’s not that same trapped feeling.

Tunnels… I guess I don’t love being in a long tunnel, but I wouldn’t plan my day around avoiding one or anything. It doesn’t really stick in my mind afterward. With elevators, I’ll be thinking about it before I even get there, like where the stairs are, how many floors, whether I can make an excuse. With cars or tunnels, I don’t really do that.

So, no, I haven’t noticed that it’s small spaces in general. It seems pretty specifically tied to elevators.
Do you ever have days where you don't think about elevators or worry about using them at all?

Yeah, there are definitely days I don’t think about them much at all. If I’m working from home or I’m just not going anywhere that involves an elevator, it’s not like it’s constantly in my head.

But once I know I might have to use one, especially at my apartment or at work with those older doors, then it pops up pretty fast. I’ll tell myself, like, this is probably safe, people use these all the time, it’s an office building or an apartment building, not some broken-down thing. But then I see the doors, and my mind just kind of treats it like, “Okay, you’re going to get trapped in there,” or “What if it drops?” And I know that sounds over the top when I’m standing here saying it, because part of me does know it’s probably fine. It’s just that in the moment, it doesn’t feel fine.
Have you always been afraid of elevators or is this something that started at some point in your life?

No, I haven’t always been afraid of them. It’s more recent than that. I’d say it started maybe around seven months ago, give or take.

It was shortly after I moved into my apartment—the one on the fifth floor—and there was this elevator scare that kind of set it off. Before that, I mean, I didn’t especially love elevators or anything, but I used them like a normal person. I didn’t really think about it much. Then after that happened, it’s like my brain started treating elevators differently, especially the one in my building. Since then it’s just sort of stuck around.
Does your fear of elevators affect your daily plans and activities every day, or are there days when it doesn't interfere at all?

It’s not every single day, no. There are plenty of days where it doesn’t really interfere, especially if I’m just going to places where I can take stairs easily or I’m not dealing with taller buildings.

But it has started affecting actual things, not just me feeling nervous. Like at work, I turned down this workshop assignment because it was in a high-rise building, and I knew I’d probably have to deal with the elevator situation. I kind of framed it like scheduling or fit or whatever, but honestly the elevator was a big reason.

And with volunteering, I used to help this older student with computer stuff, like basic computer skills, and I stopped going to see him because his building basically requires using the elevator. I mean, technically maybe there are stairs, but realistically for where he lives and the way the building is set up, it felt like I couldn’t avoid it. So I just… stopped visiting, which I don’t feel great about.

So no, it’s not ruining every day from morning to night, but when elevators are part of the plan, it can change what I agree to do.
Have you ever had a sudden, intense feeling of fear or discomfort when you were about to use an elevator or were already inside one?

Yeah, definitely. It can come on really suddenly. Like I’ll be fine walking through the lobby, or at least mostly fine, and then as soon as I start actually heading toward the elevator, it’s like my body reacts before I’ve even fully thought about it.

Especially if I hear it make that clunking sound when the doors open—like that heavy mechanical sound—my chest tightens right away. My hands get sweaty, and there’s this rush of panic that hits me really fast. It’s not like I calmly think, “Oh, I’m afraid of this,” and then slowly get nervous. It’s more immediate than that. I’ll be standing there and suddenly I feel like I need to either back away or force myself through it.

And sometimes it happens before I’m even inside. Just stepping toward it is enough. Which is frustrating, because part of me knows nothing has actually happened yet, but my body is already acting like something is wrong.
Is your fear of elevators the same for all elevators, or is it worse for certain types, like older ones or those in specific locations?

It’s definitely worse with certain elevators. I mean, if it’s a newer elevator in some office building, part of me can usually recognize, like, okay, this is probably inspected, people use it all day, it’s not actually dangerous. I don’t necessarily like it, but I can sometimes talk myself down a little.

But the older-looking ones are much worse, especially the ones with those heavy old doors, or the kind that make more noise when they open and close. Like in my apartment building, when I see those doors, my mind immediately goes to this image of being stuck inside, or the elevator suddenly dropping. And I know that sounds dramatic. I know, logically, an elevator in an office block or apartment building is probably safe. But when I’m standing there looking at it, especially if it looks worn or older, my brain doesn’t treat it like a normal safe thing. It treats it like I’m about to step into something that could trap me or fail somehow.

So, no, it’s not exactly equal across all elevators. Location matters too—my apartment building and sometimes work are worse, probably because I have to deal with them more and because the doors and the sounds just set off that whole thought pattern.
You mentioned an elevator scare that started your fear, can you tell me more about what happened during that incident?

I’m actually not totally sure how to explain it, because I don’t have one clear memory where I can say, “That was the exact incident and everything started right there.” I know I’ve probably described it as an elevator scare before, but when I try to pin it down, it’s kind of fuzzy.

I remember being scared in an elevator at some point, or at least having that feeling like something was wrong, but I don’t have a detailed, movie-like memory of what happened—like how long it lasted, who was there, what floor it was, or anything like that. It’s more like I remember the fear around it than the actual event, if that makes sense.

I don’t want to make up details just to give a better answer. What I do know is that elevators started feeling unsafe to me after that kind of experience, but I can’t really give you a clean story of, “the doors got stuck” or “it dropped” or anything specific like that. It’s more vague than I wish it was.
Is it always the sight or sound of the elevator that triggers your fear, or can it be triggered by other things as well?

It’s mostly the sight or sound, yeah, but I guess it’s not only that. The big one is still when I’m actually stepping toward it, like once I’ve decided I’m going to use it and I’m walking up to the doors. That can set it off even before anything happens.

And the sound really does it too—when it clunks open or makes that heavy mechanical noise, my body reacts almost instantly. My chest tightens, my hands get sweaty, and there’s this sudden rush of panic before I’ve even had time to think it through. It feels like my reaction is faster than my thoughts, if that makes sense.

So it’s not always just seeing it from across the lobby. Sometimes I can see an elevator and be okay-ish if I’m not going near it. But as soon as I’m moving toward it, or I hear it open, that’s when it really hits.
Is your fear of elevators always triggered by the same things, like the sight or sound of specific elevators?

Yeah, I think it’s usually the same general things, but the intensity depends on the elevator. Like I’ve said, it’s not just seeing one exists in a building. It’s more that moment when I’m actually about to use it.

As soon as I step toward an elevator, especially if I’m close enough that I’m sort of committed to getting in, my body reacts really fast. Or if I hear it clunk open—that heavy mechanical sound—my chest tightens right away, my hands get sweaty, and I get this rush of panic before I’ve even had time to think, like, “Okay, calm down, it’s probably fine.” It just happens first, and then I’m trying to catch up mentally afterward.

So I’d say the sight and sound are the big triggers, especially the doors opening or the noises it makes, but it’s also that action of moving toward it. That’s when it stops being just an elevator in the background and starts feeling like something I have to deal with.
Has your fear of elevators affected your relationships with friends or family members?

With friends and family, not as much directly, I guess. I mean, I don’t think I’ve had some big falling-out with anyone over it or anything like that. But it has started spilling into parts of my life where other people are involved.

The main examples I can think of are work and volunteering. At work, I turned down a workshop assignment because it was in a high-rise building, and I knew using the elevator was basically going to be part of it. I tried to make it sound practical, like scheduling or fit or whatever, but honestly the elevator was the real reason. That felt embarrassing, because I’m supposed to be able to handle things like that professionally.

And then with volunteering, I used to help a senior computer student, and I stopped visiting because their building basically requires taking the elevator. It’s not that I didn’t want to see them or help them anymore. I just kept putting it off, and then avoiding it, because getting up there felt like too much.

So I wouldn’t say it’s ruined my relationships, but it has affected responsibilities and commitments, and I feel bad because those involve people who were counting on me.
Has your fear of elevators caused you to avoid social gatherings or events because they are held in buildings with elevators?

Yeah, I mean… not a lot of purely social things, like parties or dinners, but it’s definitely made me avoid things when I know elevators are involved. That’s kind of why I’m here, honestly. I’ve started planning my days around not having to use them.

Like at home, I’ll take five flights of stairs instead of the elevator, even when I’m tired or carrying stuff. And at work I turned down a workshop because it was in a high-rise, and I knew there wasn’t really a way to do it without dealing with the elevator. I didn’t really say that was the reason, but it was.

And then there’s this older computer student I used to visit to help with computer stuff, and I stopped going because his building basically doesn’t give you another option. That one makes me feel bad, because it affects someone else, not just me. So, maybe not “social gatherings” exactly, but events and visits, yes—if the building means I have to use an elevator, I’ll try to get out of it or avoid it.
Do you feel like your fear of elevators is causing you a lot of distress or emotional suffering?

Yeah… I’m not totally sure how to measure “a lot,” I guess. It does bother me, but I wouldn’t say I’m falling apart over it every day or anything like that.

It’s more like this steady, frustrating thing in the background. I get embarrassed by it, especially because elevators are such a normal thing for everyone else. I’ll see people just step in without even thinking, and then I’m standing there calculating whether I can take the stairs or whether I can come up with some excuse. That part feels kind of humiliating, honestly.

So emotionally, yeah, it causes distress, but maybe not in a dramatic way. It’s more the dread beforehand, the shame afterward, and feeling annoyed with myself that something so ordinary can have that much control over what I do.
Do you feel like your fear of elevators is interfering with your ability to live your life the way you want to?

Yeah, I think it is. I don’t want to make it sound like I can’t function at all, because I can get through most days, but it’s started narrowing what I’ll agree to do.

The work thing is the clearest example. I turned down that workshop assignment because it was in a high-rise, and I knew the elevator was basically unavoidable. I told myself it was just not the right fit or that it would be inconvenient, but really I knew I was backing out because of the elevator. That bothers me because I don’t want my job choices or professional opportunities to be decided by whether a building has stairs I can realistically use.

And then with volunteering, I stopped visiting a senior computer student I used to help because their building pretty much requires taking the elevator. I kept thinking I’d go another day, or figure something out, but I just didn’t. That makes me feel worse than the work thing in some ways, because it’s someone I was supposed to be helping.

So yes, I’d say it’s interfering. Maybe not in every part of my life, but definitely in ways that matter to me.
Do you think about or worry about elevators even when you're not in a situation where you have to use one?

Yeah… I do, sometimes. Not constantly, but more than I’d like to admit.

It’s not like I’m sitting at home all day thinking about elevators out of nowhere, but if I know I have to go somewhere, I’ll start picturing the building and wondering if there’s going to be an elevator, what kind it is, whether it’s one of those older ones with the heavy doors or the sort that feels kind of shaky. And even when I’m just walking past the elevator in my apartment building or at work, my brain kind of reacts before I can talk myself out of it.

The strange part is, I know logically that an elevator in an office building is probably safe. Like, I’m not unaware of that. I know people use them all day and nothing happens. But when I look at the older doors in my apartment building, or even at work, my mind treats it like I’m about to get trapped inside or like it could suddenly drop. And part of me knows that sounds over the top, but it still feels real in the moment.

So yes, I do worry about them even before I’m actually in the situation. It’s like the elevator becomes a problem in my head before I’m even standing in front of it.
When you think about using an elevator, is your fear mainly about being trapped or is it also about something bad happening to you, like the elevator falling?

It’s both, I think. Being trapped is probably the main image that hits me first, like the doors closing and then something stopping and I can’t get out. But it’s also the falling part too, especially with older elevators.

I know, rationally, that an elevator in an office building is probably safe. I mean, people use them all day, every day, and I understand that. But when I’m actually looking at those old doors in my apartment building or at work, my brain doesn’t treat it like some normal safe machine. It treats it like I’m about to step into something that could trap me, or suddenly drop, even though part of me knows that sounds kind of extreme.

So it’s not just one fear, I guess. It’s this mix of being stuck inside and not being able to get out, plus this awful thought that something mechanical could go wrong underneath me.
Is your fear of elevators the main thing that's been causing you distress, or have you been experiencing other anxieties or fears lately?

Mostly it’s the elevators, yeah. I mean, I don’t feel like I’m generally afraid of everything or walking around scared all the time. It’s pretty specific to that situation, or even just thinking about that situation.

Like I know, in a normal part of my brain, that an elevator in an office building is probably safe. I can say that out loud and believe it, sort of. But then when I’m actually looking at the older doors in my apartment building or at work, it’s like my mind switches tracks and treats it like I’m about to step into something dangerous. I start imagining getting trapped in there, or the elevator dropping, even though another part of me knows that sounds over the top.

So I wouldn’t say there are a bunch of other fears taking over my life. The distress is mainly around elevators and all the planning and worrying that comes with avoiding them.

It’s more vague than I wish it was.

doctor.intent: determine if the fear of elevators is consistently triggered by specific stimuli
doctor.question: Is it always the sight or sound of the elevator that triggers your fear, or can it be triggered by other things as well?

target_item.name: Immediate_Fear/Anxiety_Response
target_item.manifestation: As soon as I step toward an elevator or hear it clunk open, my chest tightens, my hands get sweaty, and I feel this rush of panic before I’ve even had time to think it through.
target_item.reason: The question is asking what cues or triggers provoke the immediate fear response around elevators, which is most directly covered by the immediate fear/anxiety response profile.

patient.answer:
It’s mostly the sight or sound, yeah, but I guess it’s not only that. The big one is still when I’m actually stepping toward it, like once I’ve decided I’m going to use it and I’m walking up to the doors. That can set it off even before anything happens.

And the sound really does it too—when it clunks open or makes that heavy mechanical noise, my body reacts almost instantly. My chest tightens, my hands get sweaty, and there’s this sudden rush of panic before I’ve even had time to think it through. It feels like my reaction is faster than my thoughts, if that makes sense.

So it’s not always just seeing it from across the lobby. Sometimes I can see an elevator and be okay-ish if I’m not going near it. But as soon as I’m moving toward it, or I hear it open, that’s when it really hits.

doctor.intent: determine if the fear is consistently triggered by the same stimuli
doctor.question: Is your fear of elevators always triggered by the same things, like the sight or sound of specific elevators?

target_item.name: Immediate_Fear/Anxiety_Response
target_item.manifestation: As soon as I step toward an elevator or hear it clunk open, my chest tightens, my hands get sweaty, and I feel this rush of panic before I’ve even had time to think it through.
target_item.reason: The question is asking what triggers the fear response and whether the sight or sound of elevators provokes it, which directly matches the immediate anxiety response to the phobic situation.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I think it’s usually the same general things, but the intensity depends on the elevator. Like I’ve said, it’s not just seeing one exists in a building. It’s more that moment when I’m actually about to use it.

As soon as I step toward an elevator, especially if I’m close enough that I’m sort of committed to getting in, my body reacts really fast. Or if I hear it clunk open—that heavy mechanical sound—my chest tightens right away, my hands get sweaty, and I get this rush of panic before I’ve even had time to think, like, “Okay, calm down, it’s probably fine.” It just happens first, and then I’m trying to catch up mentally afterward.

So I’d say the sight and sound are the big triggers, especially the doors opening or the noises it makes, but it’s also that action of moving toward it. That’s when it stops being just an elevator in the background and starts feeling like something I have to deal with.

doctor.intent: determine if the fear of elevators is impacting the patient's social relationships
doctor.question: Has your fear of elevators affected your relationships with friends or family members?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: It has started affecting my work and volunteering because I turned down a high-rise workshop assignment and stopped visiting a senior computer student whose building basically requires the elevator.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the elevator fear has caused impairment in social relationships, which is most directly about functional impairment.

patient.answer:
With friends and family, not as much directly, I guess. I mean, I don’t think I’ve had some big falling-out with anyone over it or anything like that. But it has started spilling into parts of my life where other people are involved.

The main examples I can think of are work and volunteering. At work, I turned down a workshop assignment because it was in a high-rise building, and I knew using the elevator was basically going to be part of it. I tried to make it sound practical, like scheduling or fit or whatever, but honestly the elevator was the real reason. That felt embarrassing, because I’m supposed to be able to handle things like that professionally.

And then with volunteering, I used to help a senior computer student, and I stopped visiting because their building basically requires taking the elevator. It’s not that I didn’t want to see them or help them anymore. I just kept putting it off, and then avoiding it, because getting up there felt like too much.

So I wouldn’t say it’s ruined my relationships, but it has affected responsibilities and commitments, and I feel bad because those involve people who were counting on me.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's fear of elevators is causing significant distress or impairment in social or occupational areas of life
doctor.question: Has your fear of elevators caused you to avoid social gatherings or events because they are held in buildings with elevators?

target_item.name: Phobic_Avoidance_Endure
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because I’ve started planning my days around not using elevators—taking five flights of stairs at home, turning down a workshop in a high-rise, and even stopping visits with one of my older computer students because his building doesn’t really have another option.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether elevator fear leads to avoiding events or gatherings in buildings with elevators, which directly concerns active avoidance of the phobic situation.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I mean… not a lot of purely social things, like parties or dinners, but it’s definitely made me avoid things when I know elevators are involved. That’s kind of why I’m here, honestly. I’ve started planning my days around not having to use them.

Like at home, I’ll take five flights of stairs instead of the elevator, even when I’m tired or carrying stuff. And at work I turned down a workshop because it was in a high-rise, and I knew there wasn’t really a way to do it without dealing with the elevator. I didn’t really say that was the reason, but it was.

And then there’s this older computer student I used to visit to help with computer stuff, and I stopped going because his building basically doesn’t give you another option. That one makes me feel bad, because it affects someone else, not just me. So, maybe not “social gatherings” exactly, but events and visits, yes—if the building means I have to use an elevator, I’ll try to get out of it or avoid it.

doctor.intent: determine if the fear of elevators is causing significant distress
doctor.question: Do you feel like your fear of elevators is causing you a lot of distress or emotional suffering?

target_item.reason: The question asks specifically about distress or emotional suffering caused by the elevator fear, but the provided symptom profiles cover phobic fear, immediate anxiety response, avoidance, functional impairment, and duration, without a distinct item for subjective distress/emotional suffering.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I’m not totally sure how to measure “a lot,” I guess. It does bother me, but I wouldn’t say I’m falling apart over it every day or anything like that.

It’s more like this steady, frustrating thing in the background. I get embarrassed by it, especially because elevators are such a normal thing for everyone else. I’ll see people just step in without even thinking, and then I’m standing there calculating whether I can take the stairs or whether I can come up with some excuse. That part feels kind of humiliating, honestly.

So emotionally, yeah, it causes distress, but maybe not in a dramatic way. It’s more the dread beforehand, the shame afterward, and feeling annoyed with myself that something so ordinary can have that much control over what I do.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's fear of elevators is impacting their daily life to the extent that it could be considered debilitating
doctor.question: Do you feel like your fear of elevators is interfering with your ability to live your life the way you want to?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: It has started affecting my work and volunteering because I turned down a high-rise workshop assignment and stopped visiting a senior computer student whose building basically requires the elevator.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the elevator fear interferes with daily life and desired functioning, which directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I think it is. I don’t want to make it sound like I can’t function at all, because I can get through most days, but it’s started narrowing what I’ll agree to do.

The work thing is the clearest example. I turned down that workshop assignment because it was in a high-rise, and I knew the elevator was basically unavoidable. I told myself it was just not the right fit or that it would be inconvenient, but really I knew I was backing out because of the elevator. That bothers me because I don’t want my job choices or professional opportunities to be decided by whether a building has stairs I can realistically use.

And then with volunteering, I stopped visiting a senior computer student I used to help because their building pretty much requires taking the elevator. I kept thinking I’d go another day, or figure something out, but I just didn’t. That makes me feel worse than the work thing in some ways, because it’s someone I was supposed to be helping.

So yes, I’d say it’s interfering. Maybe not in every part of my life, but definitely in ways that matter to me.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's fear of elevators is persistent and pervasive enough to be considered a specific phobia
doctor.question: Do you think about or worry about elevators even when you're not in a situation where you have to use one?

target_item.name: Specific_Phobic_Fear
target_item.manifestation: I know an elevator in an office block is probably safe, but when I look at those old doors in my apartment building or at work, my mind treats it like I’m about to get trapped or dropped, even though part of me knows that sounds over the top.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about fear or worry related to elevators even outside direct use, which most directly matches the marked fear/anxiety about the specific phobic situation.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I do, sometimes. Not constantly, but more than I’d like to admit.

It’s not like I’m sitting at home all day thinking about elevators out of nowhere, but if I know I have to go somewhere, I’ll start picturing the building and wondering if there’s going to be an elevator, what kind it is, whether it’s one of those older ones with the heavy doors or the sort that feels kind of shaky. And even when I’m just walking past the elevator in my apartment building or at work, my brain kind of reacts before I can talk myself out of it.

The strange part is, I know logically that an elevator in an office building is probably safe. Like, I’m not unaware of that. I know people use them all day and nothing happens. But when I look at the older doors in my apartment building, or even at work, my mind treats it like I’m about to get trapped inside or like it could suddenly drop. And part of me knows that sounds over the top, but it still feels real in the moment.

So yes, I do worry about them even before I’m actually in the situation. It’s like the elevator becomes a problem in my head before I’m even standing in front of it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's fear is exclusively related to the fear of being trapped or if it also includes fear of other consequences like injury from malfunction
doctor.question: When you think about using an elevator, is your fear mainly about being trapped or is it also about something bad happening to you, like the elevator falling?

target_item.name: Specific_Phobic_Fear
target_item.manifestation: I know an elevator in an office block is probably safe, but when I look at those old doors in my apartment building or at work, my mind treats it like I’m about to get trapped or dropped, even though part of me knows that sounds over the top.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the specific content of the elevator fear—being trapped or the elevator falling—which matches the marked phobic fear described in this item.

patient.answer:
It’s both, I think. Being trapped is probably the main image that hits me first, like the doors closing and then something stopping and I can’t get out. But it’s also the falling part too, especially with older elevators.

I know, rationally, that an elevator in an office building is probably safe. I mean, people use them all day, every day, and I understand that. But when I’m actually looking at those old doors in my apartment building or at work, my brain doesn’t treat it like some normal safe machine. It treats it like I’m about to step into something that could trap me, or suddenly drop, even though part of me knows that sounds kind of extreme.

So it’s not just one fear, I guess. It’s this mix of being stuck inside and not being able to get out, plus this awful thought that something mechanical could go wrong underneath me.

doctor.intent: determine if the fear of elevators is the primary source of distress or if there are other underlying anxieties
doctor.question: Is your fear of elevators the main thing that's been causing you distress, or have you been experiencing other anxieties or fears lately?

target_item.name: Specific_Phobic_Fear
target_item.manifestation: I know an elevator in an office block is probably safe, but when I look at those old doors in my apartment building or at work, my mind treats it like I’m about to get trapped or dropped, even though part of me knows that sounds over the top.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the elevator fear is the primary source of distress versus other anxieties, which most directly relates to the specific phobic fear focused on elevators.

patient.answer:
Mostly it’s the elevators, yeah. I mean, I don’t feel like I’m generally afraid of everything or walking around scared all the time. It’s pretty specific to that situation, or even just thinking about that situation.

Like I know, in a normal part of my brain, that an elevator in an office building is probably safe. I can say that out loud and believe it, sort of. But then when I’m actually looking at the older doors in my apartment building or at work, it’s like my mind switches tracks and treats it like I’m about to step into something dangerous. I start imagining getting trapped in there, or the elevator dropping, even though another part of me knows that sounds over the top.

So I wouldn’t say there are a bunch of other fears taking over my life. The distress is mainly around elevators and all the planning and worrying that comes with avoiding them.
